prompt: Discuss the tension between Aristotle's claim that phantasia always involves truth-apt representation and the possibility of deceptive or erroneous imagination.

result.content:
## 1. Phantasia and Aisthesis The tension between phantasia's claim to truth-apt representation and the ever-present possibility of imaginative error begins, in Aristotle's own account, with the faculty's fraught relationship to sense-perception. Aristotle insists that "imagination is not sense" and clarifies the distinction through an appeal to experiential absence: "Sense is either a faculty or an activity, e.g. sight or seeing: imagination takes place in the absence of both, as e.g. in dreams" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 42). This passage establishes the foundational contrast: whereas aisthesis requires the present actuality of a sensible object, phantasia operates precisely where sensation has lapsed — in sleep, in memory, in anticipation. Yet this capacity to function in the absence of sensation is also the condition that opens phantasia to falsity; removed from the corrective constraint of the object's immediate presence, the image-making faculty becomes susceptible to distortion. Indeed, the very autonomy that distinguishes phantasia from aisthesis is simultaneously the source of its epistemic vulnerability. Dorothea Frede underscores this structural ambiguity by observing that Nussbaum's attempt to reduce phantasia to "just another aspect of sense-perception" cannot explain "how the function of interpreting in the wider sense that she ascribes to phantasia… can be fulfilled by a psychological process that is nothing but a secondary motion ensuing upon sense-perception" (Frede, *The Cognitive Role of Phantasia in Aristotle*, p. 6). Accordingly, phantasia must be understood as causally derived from aisthesis yet functionally autonomous — a movement (κίνησις) set in train by actual sensation that persists beyond the perceptual encounter itself. Christina Papachristou prefers to leave the Greek term untranslated, noting that "even though the Greek word 'phantasia' is usually translated… as 'imagination', I prefer to leave the word untranslated" (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 9–10), thereby signaling that the concept resists simple assimilation to modern notions of imagination. The internal distinctions within phantasia — sensory versus deliberative grades, and the faculty's complex relation to belief (doxa) and voluntariness — will be examined more fully in the sections that follow, yet even at this preliminary stage the essential paradox is visible: phantasia inherits from perception a claim to represent what is, while its independence from the perceptual object's constraining presence renders that claim perpetually insecure. 

## 2. Phantasma and Phantasia The relationship between phantasia as a faculty and the phantasma as its product intensifies the epistemological difficulty, for the image (φάντασμα) carries the representational content through which the soul engages absent objects and yet, as a residual trace of sensation, inevitably admits of deformation. Victor Caston draws attention to this problem when Aristotle acknowledges phantasia's capacity for falsity by observing that "a scene-painting or a dream are both 'something, but not what they produce a phantasia of'" (Caston, *Why Aristotle Needs Imagination*, pp. 15–16). The phantasma, thus, is genuinely something — it possesses ontological standing as a psychological event — and yet it may represent its object incorrectly; indeed, Aristotle explicitly concedes that "phantasia can be false" (Caston, *Why Aristotle Needs Imagination*, pp. 15–16). This admission is deeply consequential, for if every exercise of phantasia generates a phantasma that may or may not correspond to what is, then the faculty's claim to truth-aptness is better understood as a structural orientation toward representation rather than a guarantee of accuracy. Kevin White's analysis of *De Anima* III.3–8 enriches this point by arguing that the persistence of past sensory traces in phantasia creates a psychological tension between present sensation and past-derived imagery, such that the phantasma may conflict with what is actually perceived (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, p. 23). Kenneth Burke, writing within a rhetorical tradition that inherits the Aristotelian vocabulary, resists the dismissal of imagination as merely "overly psychologistic and extraliterary in its origins" (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 97–99), suggesting that the phantasma's representational power extends into the domain of persuasion. The distinction between sensory phantasia, which produces images closely tracking perceptual experience, and deliberative phantasia, which combines images in the service of practical reasoning, is thus already implicated in the phantasma's ambiguous epistemic status; a fuller treatment of this graded structure will be deferred to a subsequent chapter on deliberative imagination. 

## 3. Phantasia and Mneme Memory (μνήμη) discloses yet another dimension of the tension between phantasia's truth-aptness and its liability to error, for remembering requires the re-presentation of what is absent through a phantasma that purports to be of the past. John Bowin observes that Aristotle does not clearly "distinguish between remembering time and perceiving time as it is passing" (Bowin, *Aristotle on the Perception and Cognition of Time*, pp. 8–10), a remark that illuminates the peculiar temporality of the memorial phantasma: it must faithfully encode the pastness of the original experience even as it is encountered in the living present. The phantasma thus functions simultaneously as an image and as a temporal index, and this double duty magnifies the risk of distortion. If the phantasma is merely a residual motion from a prior perception, its fidelity to the original encounter degrades over time; hence the well-known phenomenon of false memory, in which the soul takes a phantasma to be of something it was not. Aristotle's treatment of deliberative phantasia — found "only in those that are calculative: for whether this or that shall be enacted is already a task requiring calculation" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 52) — underscores that even the higher-order imaginative operations depend upon memorial phantasmata to furnish their deliberative content. Burke's observation that imagination serves to "recommend the dictates of reason to imagination, in order to excite the appetite and will" (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 93–96) reveals memory's rhetorical dimension: past images are marshaled to move the soul toward action. The voluntariness initially attributed to phantasia — that images are "up to us" — is thereby complicated, since memories arise unbidden and their phantasmata may be involuntarily distorted, a point Frede acknowledges when dreams are not up to us despite being exercises of phantasia (Frede, *The Cognitive Role of Phantasia in Aristotle*, p. 6). 

## 4. Phantasia and Doxa The relationship between phantasia and doxa (δόξα) constitutes perhaps the most acute point of tension in Aristotle's account, for belief carries an intrinsic claim to truth or falsity that phantasia seems simultaneously to share and to resist. White argues that "Aristotle's first indication distinguishing phantasia from thinking is that phantasia is under voluntary control while doxa involves a reference beyond us that makes it true or false" (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, p. 23); yet this initial distinction dissolves under pressure, since phantasmata also represent — and misrepresent — states of affairs. Gonzalez's analysis of phantasia in the *Rhetoric* illuminates the problem from a different angle: in the rhetorical context, what appears (φαίνεται) to the hearer may diverge from what is actually the case, and Aristotle acknowledges that such appearances are always "πρὸς τὸν ἀκροατήν," directed toward the listener, whose doxa may be shaped accordingly (Gonzalez, *The Meaning and Function of Phantasia in Aristotle's 'Rhetoric' III.1*, pp. 14–15). O'Gorman corroborates this connection between lexis and phantasia by noting that "bringing before the eyes" constitutes a lexical form of energeia, a mode of making the absent vividly present through the mind's capacity for seeing objects in action (O'Gorman, *Aristotle's Phantasia in the Rhetoric*, p. 5). Heidegger's treatment of the πάθη as dispositions concerning "a disposition of living things in their world, in the mode of being positioned toward something, allowing a matter to matter to it" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 96–98) enriches the analysis further, for the phantasma through which doxa is formed is always already affectively colored — never a neutral representation but one shaped by the soul's dispositional orientation. Thus the tension persists irreducibly: phantasia orients toward truth-apt representation, yet its entanglement with doxa, affect, and temporal absence ensures that the images it produces remain structurally open to error, deception, and rhetorical manipulation.
